power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: October 2023 triggered two surprise attacks for the world's Jewish communities.
The first was the October 7 th (10/7) terrorist attacks by Hamas, whereas the second was the meteoric rise in antizionism in the West.

We argue that, contrary to the antizionist claim that "antizionism is not antisemitism," antizionism represents the principal, contemporary mode of strategic antisemitism, which serves the strategic goals of multiple instigators of antizionism.
We trace the roots of antizionism, highlighting that contemporary antizionism has become increasingly normalized across Western societies.
Drawing on earlier work on collective violence, we invoke the distinction between instigators and perpetrators to help explain the drivers and consequences of the recent spike in antisemitism.

We critique early Jewish counter-messaging, which focused on asserting that "antizionism = antisemitism," and we conclude by highlighting the need for empirical research on how to effectively counter contemporary antizionist narratives.

Keywords: antisemitism, antizionism, surprise, strategic, instigators, 10/7 terrorist attack Antizionism as Strategic Antisemitism A Tale of Two Surprises In October 2023, Jews worldwide experienced not one, but two, surprise attacks.

The first was 10/7-Hamas's Operation Al-Aqsa Flood, launched on October 7 th , in which the terrorist organization and other Palestinian militant groups breached Israel by air and land, indiscriminately murdering whomever they encountered.
Among the roughly 1,200 victims were hundreds of music lovers attending the outdoor Nova music festival, elderly men and women, including Holocaust survivors, and children and babies 3 .
The assailants engaged in mass sexual violence and destroyed entire families.
Those whom they could not kill before the Israeli Defence Forces managed to gain the upper hand, they attempted to abduct, successfully capturing 251 hostages.
5    The second surprise attack, and the focus of this article, may have proven to be even more surprising.
Unlike the first, it did not manifest on a single day.
Rather, it intensified from October 8 th onward.

Whereas the first surprise attack directly afflicted Israelis, setting Israel at war, the 10/8 surprise attack-or simply 10/8-directly afflicted Jews living in Western diasporas such as Australia, Canada, France, the UK, and the US.

This second attack consisted initially in the morally incongruous support Hamas received from various quarters, such as university professors and students at elite institutions declaring their support for the attacks as a legitimate form of resistance to Israel's ostensibly colonial oppression of Palestinians.

text.text: It would not even be correct to describe it as resurgent, given that it had not waned over the interceding decades.
Rather, we might describe the antizionist response to 10/7 as escalatory.
It is the escalation of antizionism and its rapid diffusion into the broader society that triggered surprise among so many Jews worldwide.
The surprise was not only in the antizionist response to 10/7 that was observed, but in the fact that it was Israel-supporting Jews who were put on the defensive.

As noted earlier, the antizionists' line of defence-namely, that antizionism was not antisemitic, but that it was, in fact, moral and in keeping with the fight against oppression and genocide-was highly effective as an influence tactic and form of strategic deflection.
The ploy put mainstream Jews (i.e., the majority of Jews in excess of 90% who believe in Israel's right to exist as a state 44 , the foundation of Zionism 45 ) on the defensive.

text.text: Off to a bad start.

As antizionists were gathered en masse on university campuses and city streets to brand Israel as the 21 st century Nazis committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and branding diaspora Jews as privileged, 47 White racists 48 who supported Israeli genocide, diaspora Jews who were caught in a state of suspended disbelief eventually responded with their own slogan: "antizionism = antisemitism."

text.text: Thus, a predominant Jewish response to the antizionists' denial that antizionism was antisemitic was to move the denial process up one level by denying the denial, effectively triggering a game of denial ping-pong.
The rhetorical maneuver it represented was virtually guaranteed to be ineffective.

Unlike kinetic war, where a surprise attack by a weaker force could be met with an overwhelming counter-attack, in narrative warfare, each response and counter-response is a linguistic turn in an evolving narrative battle, 49 underscoring the principle that "the best defence is a good offence."

text.text: By striking the first blow, contemporary antizionists succeeded in labelling Israel as the aggressor and Zionists as racists to be openly stigmatized.
Thus, mainstream Jews were under pressure to explain why they were not racists and why Israel was not the aggressor it was claimed to be.

However, by responding to such allegations, which were coupled with the caveat that "antizionism is not antisemitism," with the counter-slogan "antizionism is antisemitism," Jews stepped into an unwinnable, rhetorical game of "am not!
/are too!"
Such a strategy neglected the fact that what was being denied by the antizionists was merely the caveat.
The central theme of the narrative focused on Israel's purported crimes and illegitimacy and the alleged moral depravity of those who supported the state.
The counter-denial, thus, did nothing to elaborate on why the central accusation against Israel and Israel-supporting Jews was wrong.
Rather than appealing to the broader societal base of bystanders, such meta-denial-based messaging ran the risk of appearing morally bereft and self-servingly tone deaf.
Even without that context, there is evidence to suggest that denials are ineffective tactics for promoting attitudinal change.

text.text: Nor should this be difficult to do, given that contemporary antizionism is not merely antisemitism, but rather, the ultimate, contemporary manifestation of strategic antisemitism-namely, antisemitism that is perpetuated to serve distinct political objectives of organized stakeholders.

Addressing the rise of antizionism as the principal expressive mode of antisemitism in the 21 st century, therefore, requires that its strategic function to those state and non-state actors it serves be analyzed and exposed.

The emphasis we place on strategic antisemitism is vital, conveying to the listener that, in the present context, antizionism refers to a form of antisemitism designed to bring about strategic aims of particular actors.
This contrasts with antisemitism, in general, which is often construed as an irrational hatred of Jews.

Though we do not deny that irrational or non-rational (e.g., emotive) psychological processes play a role in fomenting antisemitism, the focus on psychological explanations tends to overlook systemic drivers of antisemitism and, thus, may do more to obscure understanding of the topic than to clarify it.
Irrationality, at best, might be overcome through education-at worst, it must be managed as an uncorrectable cognitive defect.

However, education alone cannot overcome the challenges posed by contemporary antizionism because its instigators have acted strategically to ensure the movement expands through the weaponization of Western educational systems. 66 Klaff notes the key role that academia has played in the normalization of antizionist propaganda, adding that "[s]tudents, because of their youth, enthusiasm, and traditional political involvement, are a primary target audience for such anti-Zionist efforts." 67 Klaff further elucidates the ideological roots taken hold in academia by tracing the links of various Muslim groups and speakers to antizionist lobby groups, Hamas, and the Muslim Brotherhood.

text.text: As already noted, antizionism was weaponized by the Soviet Union after Israel's strategic alignment with the US, and much of contemporary antizionist messaging and iconography can be traced directly to Soviet-era propaganda. 78 Tabarovsky outlines how Soviet era propaganda represented Zionism as a form of racism, imperialism, and conspiracy for global domination. 79 The frequently-used slogans in post-10/7 protests equating Zionism with Nazism or colonialism were pioneered in the Soviet Union. 80 Soviet defector and former KGB propagandist, Yuri Bezmenov, detailed how Soviet propaganda strategically served in transforming mobilized Western actors into tools of the subversion process aimed at destabilizing Western democracies. 81 As well, the USSR permitted a very narrow definition of acceptable Jewry and its leaders viewed the Zionist movement as a significant threat to that control, which required antizionist countermeasures. 82 Although the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia under Putin has remained a staunch adversary of the West and the US, in particular, which remains Israel's strongest and most powerful ally.

text.text: Although the strategic use of antizionism is not a new phenomenon, the escalation of antizionist rhetoric in the West, including the constant vilification of Israel as a "Zionist entity" equal to Nazis committing genocide against Palestinians, has not only changed the quantity of such messaging, the quality has also been transformed.
Whereas before 10/7, it was seen as socially acceptable to target Israel, it was unacceptable to target mainstream Jews simply because they support Israel's right to exist.

However, it has become increasingly acceptable to harass Jews, accusing them of being evil, and to target Jewish cultural institutions. 93 Nor is the targeting restricted to verbal assaults online or in from a confusion of cause and symptom.

text.text: Examples such as those just described are symptoms.
They are expressions of antizionist antisemitism, but they are directed by strategic forces of which they are likely to be unaware.

The Neo-Marxist writer and politician, Antonio Gramsci, wrote that in Western societies, true revolution first requires a deeply embedded counter-hegemonic (ideological) movement. 98 Gramsci identifies educational and religious institutions, media, and professional associations as prime targets for counter-hegemonic movements. 99 Consistent with this pattern, the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy (ISGAP) has documented that billions of dollars of funding from Arab countries, primarily Qatar, has flowed to Western academic institutions, and that the institutions receiving this funding report high rates of antisemitism among universities. 100 While suggestive, more work is needed to document the direct linkages between these countries' strategic objectives, funding decisions, and the incentives and pressures-direct and indirect-they place on Western institutions to adopt or at least tolerate antizionism.

text.text: Care in counter-messaging must be exercised because weak counter-arguments, such as denials of emotionally-vested positions like "antizionism is not antisemitism" can backfire, inadvertently inoculating those who are moving along a path toward antisemitism against positive belief change. 103 For individuals who truly believe that Israel is a genocidal, apartheid state, or who believe that Jews are a powerful cabal controlling financial, cultural, and political capital around the world, the "antizionism = antisemitism" denial of the contemporary antizionist's purity claim will surely fall on deaf ears.

text.text: Such denials may even strengthen rather than attenuate their commitment to opposing Israel, if they perceive such efforts as the result of "powerful Jews" trying to "control the narrative."
Nor is it evident that such messaging is effective at reducing the susceptibility of individuals to antizionist antisemitism among those who have not committed to an attitudinal position.
Denials without evidence or elaborations for that position might appear defensive and self-serving.

It may be better to develop a counter-narrative that explains why it has been in the strategic interest of various state and non-state actors to foster antizionism, and to explain how these stakeholders have been successful in bringing about attitudinal change in the direction of antizionist sentiment.
Drawing on research documenting the societal costs of antizionist belief contagion may ultimately prove more persuasive than issuing blanket denials.

For instance, a study by Jussim and colleagues conducted in July 2023 (namely, months before 10/7) of over 100 million posts on the social media platform X found that the frequency of antizionist posts was positively correlated with the frequency of antisemitic incidents. 104 Such findings underscore that even if antizionism is not a proper subset of antisemitism, its manifestation has negative consequences for the majority of Jews.

text.text: We expect the lopsidedness of such human rights foci to have become even more extreme in the intervening years.

More generally, strategic messaging designed to counter contemporary antizionism must be rigorously, empirically tested for efficacy and harmful side effects in the same way we demand of any new drug.
All drug trials start out with hope of success and are based on what seem to the researchers at least to be sound reasoning.
Yet, many good ideas fail, and it is all too easy to be seduced by the apparent goodness of one's ideas, including being seduced into thinking that empirical tests are not needed.
However, randomly controlled trials on messaging interventions are desperately needed.
Unfortunately, such tests are seldom performed.
Instead, messaging campaigns often rely on little more than what their developers believe will work.
Such idea entrepreneurs often have unrealistic beliefs regarding the probability of success.

For instance, a recent study found that a significantly greater proportion of American participants exposed to typical Anti-Defamation League (ADL) antioppressive, anti-hate messaging expressed antisemitic views than participants who were exposed to either ADL hate statistics, control messaging (about corn), Judaism, or messaging emphasizing American shared values. 106 Such results are concerning given that the ADL is one of the best-funded agencies tasked with fighting antisemitism.

text.text: Clearly, antisemitism cannot be fought with messaging that inadvertently promotes an antisemitic response.
Resources spent on counter-messaging campaigns that backfire are wasteful and damaging.
The problem is not new.

Twenty-five years ago, Dawidowicz summarized the many ways, both intentional and unintentional, that Holocaust education could misinform students, teach them the wrong lessons about the Holocaust, and exploit the Holocaust for other "noble" purposes. 107 Nor is the problem restricted to this domain.

text.text: Skeptical priors regarding solution success rates motivate testing rather than rapid (and often premature) adoption of techniques and policies.
This is all the more important post-10/7, when Jewish communities face escalating attacks and feel pressured to find quick solutions to ameliorate the problem.

Thus, in tandem with a skeptical disposition, we need multiple, independent, and well-funded programs of applied experimental research on attitudinal change to test what seem to be the best ideas for combating contemporary antizionism and antisemitism while simultaneously promoting a resurgence of support for Western liberal values.
